newsitem.title: BOSNIA: FEATURE - Donors debate fine-tuning Bosnian aid.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Donors debate fine-tuning Bosnian aid.

text.p: Bosnian Serbs who flout the Dayton peace accord by refusing to surrender war criminals and blocking returning refugees may get more than a billion dollars in international aid anyway, diplomats say.
"We're at a turning point for the reconstruction programme and for the peace process as a whole," a western diplomat in Sarajevo, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.

"There's a developing consensus among donors that witholding economic aid to force compliance on war criminals has not worked and will not work. If the stick isn't effective perhaps it's time to try the carrot."

Political conditions for aid are among the many thorny issues to be considered at a "Dayton Two" conference in London next week, where world leaders will gather to fine tune the Bosnian peace process as it heads into its second year.

The international community actually spent about $728 million on reconstruction projects in Bosnia in the first 11 months of the peace process, 98 percent of which went to the country's Moslem-Croat Federation.

Post-war aid until the end of the century is scheduled to amount to $5.1 billion. Of that, $1.4 billion has tentatively been allocated to the Bosnian Serbs' Republika Srpska, which controls 49 percent of the country.
The goal of the aid programme is to move Bosnia from near- total dependence to self-support.

Mediators say the Federation's record on compliance with the peace accord signed in Dayton, Ohio, last November has been patchy at best, but better than that of Republika Srpska, which openly rejects many key elements of the agreement.
"Frankly, conditionality hasn't been working on either side," said Swedish mediator Carl Bildt, who coordinates the civilian side of the peace process.
"The Federation is convinced money will flow to it no matter what and Republika Srpska is convinced it won't receive aid under any circumstances. There needs to be a balance."
Ordinary citizens in Republika Srpska are paying a heavy price for their leaders' post-war adherence to the politics of ethnic separatism.
The World Bank reports wages three times higher on the Federation side of Bosnia than on the Serb side and near-zero inflation compared to an annual rate in Srpska between 35 and 65 percent.
What is more, economic pump priming by the world community has generated an overall growth rate of 35-50 percent in the Federation while growth within Republika Srpska is either zero or negative.

"Lack of investment...is causing immense hardship and anguish for the people of Srpska and I think that the donor community will take that into account," said Rory O'Sullivan, director of World Bank operations in Bosnia.
The World Bank, a big donor in Bosnia and coordinator of many other donors' funds, prefers to focus on the economic merit rather than the political merit of prospective projects.
Critics accuse the international community of squandering legitimate leverage over egregious violators of Dayton, making a mockery of the peace accords and cementing the country's de facto partition.

"It's ridiculous. The message being sent is: slaughter, expel, destroy and then wait a decent interval and the world community will send money to you," said Chris Bennett, an analyst with the International Crisis Group (ICG).
"We think it's disastrous not to have strict conditionality on every element of economic assistance.

"Without strict conditionality we'll see a repeat of (the Bosnian city of) Mostar, where the European Union recently spent 264 million marks ($173 million) to unify a city which remains partitioned between Moslems and Croats."

Many aid experts say that while conditionality may be effective at the political margin in Bosnia, none of the factions can be bought off when it comes to core principles, however perverse those principles may seem to outsiders.
Richard Sklar, U.S. special envoy to Bosnia for reconstruction, divides points of potential aid leverage into three tiers: the impossible, the possible and the necessary.

Category "A" -- conditions he reckons impossible to attain by witholding aid -- includes the surrender of war criminals and the right of refugees to return to areas where they would be ethnic minorities.
"I am not optimistic, no matter what is done here other than applying draconian economic measures or the direct use of force, that you are going to make progress on category "A"," Sklar told Reuters.
Category "B" includes possibly achievable conditions such as freedom of movement, open media and free elections.
And Category "C", which Sklar terms "prosaic but necessary and do-able", includes technical criteria directly relevant to the project at hand.

For instance, any water project funded by the international community now has to include international review of design, a leak prevention programme and a user fee to cover future operating and maintenace costs, among other requirments.
In Sklar's view Categories "B" and "C" are the proper targets of conditioned aid. Those in Category "A" are more the province of NATO troops and the U.N. police.
"If you apply rigid rules that say you must comply with all aspects of Dayton, no aid will go to anyone because all three sides are in violation of political conditions," Sklar said.
"We call this the Bahamas option. All of us working on the reconstruction programme could head for the Bahamas because nothing would ever happen here." ($1=1.5255 Mark)
